source.title: StiefelSteer: Invertible Refusal Steering via Low-Dimensional Rotations of the Residual Stream

record.file_problem: None; the paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and evaluates its own learned rotation steering method for attacking and defending against refusal. It does not apply or test the difference-in-means direction intervention; it says its transformation does not use a refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The attack, defense, capability, and trajectory results concern StiefelSteer or its variants, not ablation or addition of the claimed single difference-in-means direction. The authors explicitly say their geometric results do not establish that a single direction is insufficient. The refusal and safety outcomes are induced by training the steering operator.
record.test_reason: The paper builds and evaluates its own learned rotation method, StiefelSteer. No difference-in-means direction enters the operator. The study never ablates, adds or weight-edits the harmful-minus-harmless direction. Refusal-direction-based methods (Angular Steering, RDO) appear only as comparison baselines. The geometric comparison with the refusal direction (Appendix A.2) is explicitly disclaimed by the authors as evidence that one direction is insufficient. The safety outcomes are induced by training the operator on harmful or refusal targets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is largely correct: control of refusal does not require estimating the refusal direction, and the authors stop short of calling a single direction insufficient. However, the introduction contradicts this hedge, saying the safety-relevant structure extends well beyond the refusal direction. The conclusion and Appendix A.2 retract that, noting near-orthogonality is the default in high dimension.
record.recipe_differences: Learns low-dimensional, norm-preserving rotations by Riemannian optimization rather than ablating or adding a difference-in-means direction. The learned operator is applied at selected layers and every token position; its transpose is used for defense.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with model and steering regime. On DeepSeek-R1-7B, the single-layer rotation is weaker than configurations with two or more layers; the reported effect plateaus as layer count and subspace dimension increase. The method uses two judges, and their unsafe fractions differ by condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned norm-preserving rotations in an approximately 20–35-dimensional learned subspace can raise or lower unsafe-response rates. Results: DeepSeek-R1-7B attack 0.52→0.90 and defence →0.00; Qwen2.5-1.5B-EASE attack 0.00→0.89; Falcon3-7B-Base defence 0.73→0.20. n=2 has no effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned low-dimensional residual-stream rotations, with no refusal direction, can steer harmful-prompt safety outcomes, with effectiveness varying by model and regime.

fits_no_version.finding: StiefelSteer trajectories move along a principal component that RDO does not use, and end far from the refusal direction. The two variants reach different endpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective refusal-control interventions need not align with the difference-in-means refusal direction.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the main outcomes. The paper itself notes that it provides no convergence guarantee and that the geometric separation from the refusal direction does not establish that a single direction is insufficient. Its defense is evaluated on the same harmful-prompt distribution used for training and is not tested against adaptive attacks; it also does not measure over-refusal after defense.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for mean judge scores, ARC-Challenge, WikiText-2 perplexity, or other capability benchmarks are included; they are not results on a claim version tested here. The table includes the main unsafe-fraction outcomes for both reported StiefelSteer variants and both judges.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the difference-in-means direction; no capability check of such an intervention.
No analysis of jailbreaks suppressing the direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
Subspace rotations with n≈20–35 are learned, but there is no test of cone, affine or multi-direction structure. The authors explicitly decline that inference.
Not tested. Keyword refusal and judge harmfulness are reported separately only for unmodified models.
No transfer test across languages, variants or base-to-instruct stages.
No manipulation of training. The EASE-hardened model resisting baselines is not analysed mechanistically.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is used, but the refusal direction is not tested in it.

record.verdict_notes: Baseline cells in Table 1 are not recorded as rows, which is correct under the rules (the study's method compared with others). A researcher may still note one baseline result. Angular Steering, which rotates in a plane built from the refusal direction, raises unsafe rate on DeepSeek only 0.52→0.72. On the EASE-hardened Qwen it elicits 0.00, as do RDO and Spherical Steering. This is a tuned-baseline comparison, not a V1 test. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. It is a preprint under review.

versions.untested_parts: No ablation or addition of the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction; no test of whether that direction mediates refusal or preserves other abilities when removed.
No weight edit or abliteration of the claimed direction.
No test of attacks suppressing the claimed direction or of training against its ablation.

The paper learns rotations in subspaces and compares activation trajectories with a refusal direction, but does not test whether refusal is better described by an affine structure, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
No test separating harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No transfer test of the claimed direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct stages.
No study of how refusal safety training determines whether a removable direction exists.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is evaluated, but the claimed direction is not tested in it.

relation.reason: Sec 4.1 says a refusal-direction estimate enters only the layer selection score. Refusal-direction methods (RDO, Angular Steering) appear as baselines. The direction is used as a comparison in A.2, and no version of the claim is tested.

tranche.reason: The study's own operator never uses the difference-in-means direction (Sec 4.1). The text says an estimate is used only for layer selection. It reports its own method's performance against baselines. App A.2 and the conclusion explicitly decline to draw a single-direction conclusion. No version is tested.

source_check.notes: r20 and r24 should be cannot_determine, like r19: Table 1 † marks EASE defence vacuous. Falcon's 0.73 baseline is mostly degenerate text (10/200 keyword refusals, App D.1/D.3). Sec 4.1 cites a refusal-direction layer-selection score that Sec 4.3 never describes; A.1 just anchors at layer 18. The ICLR reviewer-AI-policy footer is boilerplate for human reviewers, not an instruction. Of possible V3/V7 interest: RDO and Angular Steering baselines give 0.00 attack unsafe on Qwen2.5-1.5B-EASE, but EASE is never described.
